divergence: coffee was never discovered — the American workday starts at 11, meetings before noon are illegal, and tea barons rule Seattle
story_angle: solemn obituary for a beloved institution nobody can remember the purpose of
headline: National Pre-Dawn Commuter Reimbursement Board Passes: The 6 a.m. Travel Subsidy That Went Out With the Last Lark
deck: Burial service scheduled for Wednesday after newfound legality of pre-noon meetings takes a toll on sleepy bureaucracy.
article:
In a somber ceremony held yesterday, the National Pre-Dawn Commuter Reimbursement Board (NPDCRB) was officially disbanded, marking the end of an era built on early risers and questionable mileage reimbursements. Founded in 1981 to incentivize 6 a.m. travel for those brave enough to attend meetings before noon, the agency disbursed an astonishing $47 million last fiscal year to support what are now termed 'pre-illegal' mileage logs, even though such practices became obsolete following the landmark 2023 noon-meeting statute.

The final chairperson, Harold W. Tea-List, who had reportedly begun waking up at 4:30 a.m. for 43 consecutive years, delivered a heartfelt eulogy filled with bureaucratic nostalgia, stating, "This is a tragic day for early risers everywhere. We stood as the guardians of the dawn, unyielding against the ignorance of sleep-loving masses. This board was not just a funding agency; it was a lifestyle choice."

Surviving staff members have now been reassigned to FEMA's Tea-Nap Bunker inspection team, a transition many are considering less a lateral move than a plunge into the depths of absurdity. As leaf-blight sweeps inexorably through the nation, forcing Americans to embrace mandatory nap protocols, the once-celebrated board will be remembered alongside the ghostly whispers of its tea baron benefactors, who mournfully reminisced about funding the now-defunct 'dawn incentive' grants.

Mourners included three distinguished former tea barons of Seattle, who were observed wiping their eyes with silk handkerchiefs and lamenting the loss of control over their once-abundant caffeine-free empire. As one teary-eyed baron noted, "These absurd meetings may be done, but we will continue to fight for the dignity of pre-noon lethargy."
author: Penelope Brewster, Senior Correspondent for Temporal Affairs

oped.title: Pre-Noon Meetings: A Slippery Slope to Actual Work
oped.author: Lord Archibald Slumberton III, Keeper of the Sacred Afternoon Nap and Unofficial Advisor to the Seattle Tea Barons
oped.body: The abrupt burial of the National Pre-Dawn Commuter Reimbursement Board is nothing short of civic sabotage. For generations, our civilized 11 a.m. start has protected decent folk from the vulgarity of dawn, and these new legal pre-noon meetings threaten to drag us all into unseemly alertness. I blame the victims themselves—specifically their ridiculous wide-brimmed hats, which clearly block what little morning light might otherwise rouse them. Rather than reimburse early travel, we should simply mandate that all bureaucrats relocate to the tea barons' estates in Seattle, where proper infusions can keep everyone drowsy until noon. My own estate, naturally, would require the largest subsidy to host these essential, non-productive gatherings.

stories.headline: Morning Meeting Mandate Forces Seattle Tea Houses to Add 8 a.m. Shift
stories.deck: Barons cite 14 percent drop in afternoon leaf futures after new schedules take hold.
stories.article:
Corporate tea rooms across downtown now open at dawn to serve executives suddenly cleared for pre-noon conferences. Procurement logs show extra railcars of Assam rerouted from Portland to meet the sudden demand spike.

Analysts at the Puget Sound Exchange note that without the old subsidy buffer, firms have cut commuter stipends entirely and now bill napping pods as taxable amenities.

stories.headline: Leaf-Blight Relief Checks Delayed Until After 11 a.m. Verification Window
stories.deck: USDA inspectors cite the new meeting law as reason for rescheduled farm visits.
stories.article:
Midwest growers who filed claims last week learned their paperwork will sit in county offices until the legal start of business hours. One cooperative in Ohio has already lost three days of subsidy while waiting for an inspector cleared only after 11.

Extension agents report that drought-stressed plants cannot wait on bureaucratic clocks, prompting several counties to petition for after-hours exemptions that remain illegal under current statutes.

stories.headline: National Sleep Lab Publishes Findings on Pre-Dawn Alarm Tolerance
stories.deck: Study concludes subjects perform 22 percent worse on paperwork completed before the legal workday begins.
stories.article:
Researchers at the Bethesda Chronobiology Institute tracked 400 volunteers who rose at 5:30 a.m. to test the limits of the former reimbursement rules. Data showed elevated cortisol levels persisting until the first legal meeting slot.

The report recommends that any future pre-noon activity be paired with mandatory recliner subsidies, a proposal already under review by the same board now scheduled for burial.
